Yes. 

The ending feels completely natural, earned, and purposeful, arriving at the exact emotional resolution the entire story has been building toward. Throughout the narrative, Nora struggles with a sense of disorientation (being "turned around" in the pinwheel-shaped ward) and an inability to feel the immediate "rush of overwhelming love" she was promised upon giving birth, describing her initial emotion instead as an unlabeled "piece of furniture delivered to the wrong address." The conversations at night with the other mothers establish the theme of the babies' strange interchangeability ("I thought, well, that one's mine, and then I thought, but why that one"). 

When Nora realizes she has been given the wrong baby, the narrative doesn't treat it as a sensational plot twist, but rather as the catalyst for her emotional breakthrough. Because this baby isn't biologically hers, the pressure of predetermined expectation vanishes, allowing her to experience an "unearned" and "purest happiness." The final line—where Nora finally sits down and lets "herself be found"—beautifully resolves the central metaphor of being lost and turned around, bringing her character arc to a deeply satisfying close.
